summary:
Rivers State lies in southern Nigeria. The sources identify no Rivers statute, policy or enforcement practice of its own on same-sex conduct or gender expression; the state stands under Nigeria's national framework, which the sources confirm reaches a visitor to Port Harcourt and the rest of Rivers. The layer that varies by geography is the Criminal Code in force across southern Nigeria, and it applies here: sex between men carries penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years.

Rivers is not among the northern states where Sharia provisions apply. The penalties reported for those states, from lashing to death, do not reach a visitor in Port Harcourt. Exposure in Rivers comes from the secular Criminal Code and the national framework rather than from Zina provisions.

The only Rivers-specific event in the sources is an assault in Port Harcourt. In January 2015 a 21-year-old gay man travelled from Lagos to the city to meet a man he had contacted on Facebook, was attacked and sexually abused there, and did not report it to the police. Human Rights Watch recorded the case in its October 2016 report 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe'. Meeting arranged online, assault by the contact, no recourse sought: all three are documented inside Rivers itself.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement by mass arrest at social venues is documented across Nigeria but not in Rivers in these sources. More than 100 party-goers were held at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018, 57 young men at Egbeda in Lagos in August 2018, 67 people in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023 and 76 at a party in Gombe in October 2023. Asaba and Warri are in Delta State, which borders Rivers, so the raid pattern sits next door even though no Rivers raid appears.

The Port Harcourt case follows the shape of the entrapment pattern that Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation documented nationally in April 2024: meetings arranged through apps or social networks where victims are beaten and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police extorting people for their appearance is sourced from elsewhere. In March 2025 TimesLIVE reported a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'. No comparable Rivers incident is sourced, so the Lagos case is the nearest evidence of how a gender-nonconforming visitor might be treated by police in the region.
localsOnly:
No legal protection for LGBTQ people exists in Rivers State, and the sources record no Rivers anti-discrimination instrument. In 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists sued over Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, and the court ruled them unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, removing those provisions as a basis for prosecuting LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals in Rivers. The ruling struck those sections only; no protection against discrimination follows from it.

Residents organising in Rivers remain exposed under the rest of the framework. Human Rights Watch assessed in October 2016 that registering, operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations carried 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, that the Act bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after it passed, including in the case of eight of the 21 young men arrested but never charged at a birthday party in Ibadan.

Reporting crime carries its own exposure. In the Port Harcourt assault the victim did not go to the police, and the sources record no prosecution, compensation or finding arising from it.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Rivers-specific arrest, raid, prosecution, venue closure or police policy appears in the sources. Whether Rivers police have used the national framework or the Criminal Code against anyone in Port Harcourt is unresolved.

Whether the 2022 ruling on Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) has been invoked in Rivers courts, or cited by Rivers police to decline a prosecution, is unresolved. The sources give the nationwide effect of the ruling but no Rivers docket.

Nothing in the sources addresses trans-specific incidents, document or marker rules, screening practice, bathroom and facility access, or healthcare availability in Rivers State. The trans-specific violence, imprisonment and official-misgendering record in the wider inventory concerns Abuja and Lagos, not Rivers.

The sources do not describe LGBTQ+ venues, organisations, support services or HIV programmes operating in Port Harcourt today. The documented closure of an LGBTQ-friendly church concerns Lagos, and no Rivers equivalent is recorded.
